hints: Think about the carbonyl group ($C=O$) and ask yourself which functional group each molecule is famous for: aldehyde in a sugar, alcohol in glycerol, amide in a peptide bond.

Recall that glucose in its open-chain form has an aldehyde group, proteins are full of peptide bonds with the pattern $-CO-NH-$, but glycerol has only three $-OH$ alcohol groups with single $C-O$ bonds.
walkthrough:
**Recall what C=O means**

Think carbonyl. A double bond between carbon and oxygen appears in aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and amides.

Look for: $C=O$

**Check glucose and glycerol**

Glucose is an aldose sugar. Its straight-chain form has an aldehyde group at carbon 1, so it definitely contains $C=O$.

Glycerol is propane-1,2,3-triol: $CH_2OH-CHOH-CH_2OH$. It has only $C-C$, $C-H$, $C-O$ single bonds and $O-H$ groups. No $C=O$ at all, so statement 2 is out.

**Check protein**

A protein is a long chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Each peptide bond is formed by condensation and has the structure $-CO-NH-$.

That $CO$ part is a $C=O$ double bond, so statement 3 is in. That leaves 1 and 3 only.

options.A: Incorrect because glycerol (2) has only alcohol groups with single C-O bonds and no C=O, so all three cannot be correct.
options.B: Incorrect because while glucose (1) is correct, glycerol (2) has no C=O and protein (3) does have C=O in its peptide bonds.
options.C: Correct because glucose has an aldehyde C=O and protein has C=O in every peptide bond, while glycerol has none.
options.D: Incorrect because glycerol (2) lacks C=O, so it cannot be included with protein (3).
